definition: The push a seat or restraint gives a rider compared with sitting still, expressed as a multiple of gravity.
The floating feeling near zero g when the track drops away faster than gravity pulls the rider.
Sideways force on a rider in a turn, reduced by banking the track.
The rate at which acceleration changes; sudden jerk makes muscles overshoot and heads whip.
Dimming, colourless vision caused by sustained positive g draining blood from the head.
A closed region of allowed combined accelerations, by duration, that a ride must stay inside.
A spiral whose curvature grows in proportion to distance along it, used for loops and transitions.
The roll axis chosen to pass through the average rider's chest so that rolls feel nearly force-free.
The railway term for banking: raising the outer rail of a curve so the force comes through the seat.
A length of track where curvature and bank ramp gradually between a straight and a curve.
Rocky Mountain Construction's steel track of paired I-beams that bolts to wooden supports.
Energy lost as a tyre squashes and recovers on the rail, a small fraction of the wheel load.
A pivoting hook under the train that catches the lift chain.
A spot where a slow train runs out of momentum and rolls back to the low point, stranding riders.
A section of track with its own stop and start control; only one train may occupy it.
A brake that slows a train to manage speed or forces but cannot stop it.
A contactless brake in which magnets induce currents in a moving fin, producing drag that rises with speed.
A pivoting pawl under the car that drops into a ratchet so the train can climb but never slide back.
An inductive sensor that detects a metal flag passing without contact, used to count cars.
A wheel running under the rail that stops the train lifting off in inversions and over hills.
A sliding or rotating track section that moves trains onto a storage or maintenance siding.
A plot of stress range against cycles to failure used to predict fatigue life.
Coating steel by dipping it in molten zinc, which protects as a barrier and sacrificially.
A crash-test score computed from the head's acceleration over a short window, used to compare coasters with other activities.
Repeated strikes of the head against a hard restraint caused by lateral jolts on a rough ride.
